concepts.title: Why Chunking Comes Before Embedding
concepts.description: Before any vector is computed, documents have to be broken into pieces. Embedding models enforce their own token limits, and compressing an entire multi-topic document into one vector blurs everything it discusses together, which hurts retrieval even when no length limit applies.
learningObjectives: Explain why embedding models have a fixed maximum input length, and describe what typically happens, often with no error, when an input exceeds it.
Distinguish the embedding model's own context window limit from the generation LLM's context window limit, and explain why solving one does not solve the other.
Explain the retrieval-granularity problem: why compressing an entire multi-topic document into a single vector produces mediocre similarity scores for queries about any one of its subtopics.
Predict the consequence of silently truncating a document during embedding, and explain why that failure produces no error and no warning.
Explain why chunking is a deliberate, offline preprocessing decision made once per document, before any embedding call happens at all.

sections.heading: Two Separate Context Windows, Two Separate Problems
sections.body:
Once a generation model offers a context window of 128,000 tokens or more, it's easy to assume context limits are a solved problem for a RAG pipeline and that chunking only mattered when models were smaller. That skips over a separate component with its own, usually much smaller, limit: the **embedding model** that builds the searchable index. Many widely used sentence-embedding models cap their input at somewhere between 256 and 512 tokens, and even hosted embedding APIs typically stop in the low thousands, nowhere near the generation model's window. These are two independent limits, enforced by two different models doing two different jobs, and raising (or forgetting about) one tells you nothing about the other.

What happens when you hand an encoder more tokens than it accepts depends on the library and model. Some hosted APIs reject the request with an error, but a common default elsewhere (sentence-transformers, for example, cuts input at the model's maximum sequence length) is to truncate: keep the first N tokens, discard the rest, raise nothing.

```python
def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def truncate(tokens, max_tokens):
    return tokens[:max_tokens]

def toy_embed(text, max_tokens=8):
    # Stand-in for a real encoder's internal truncate-then-embed behavior.
    # Everything past max_tokens is never looked at.
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    truncated = truncate(tokens, max_tokens)
    seed = sum(len(t) for t in truncated)
    return [(seed % 5) / 5, (seed % 7) / 7]

document = (
    "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent driven "
    "primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March "
    "which exceeded internal projections"
)

print(len(tokenize(document)))            # 23: the document length
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8))   # only the first 8 tokens are ever seen
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100)) # the full document, for comparison
```

The truncated call doesn't fail or warn, and returns something that looks like every other embedding vector the pipeline produces. Whatever the document said about the enterprise product line, the internal projections, or anything past word 8 is never seen by the model, in this toy example and in many real libraries running with default settings.

sections.heading: The Retrieval-Granularity Problem: Chunking Matters Even Without a Length Limit
sections.body:
Suppose an embedding model had no length limit and could accept an entire 50-page document as one input. Chunking would still be necessary, for a reason unrelated to token limits: a single fixed-length vector has to represent everything the document talks about at once, and averaging several unrelated subtopics produces a vector that represents each of them only weakly.

Recall how encoders produce a document-level vector: pooling (commonly averaging) many per-token contextual vectors down into one fixed-length result. If a document discusses billing, security, and onboarding in roughly equal measure, its pooled vector sits somewhere in the geometric middle of all three topics, near each of them but not nearly as near to any one as a vector for *only* that topic would be:

```python
def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sum(x * x for x in a) ** 0.5
    nb = sum(y * y for y in b) ** 0.5
    return dot / (na * nb)

# Illustrative topic vectors, not computed by a real encoder.
topic_billing = [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0]
topic_security = [0.0, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]
topic_onboarding = [0.0, 0.0, 0.9, 0.1]

# A whole-document vector that discusses all three topics, pooled together.
whole_doc_vector = [
    sum(v[i] for v in (topic_billing, topic_security, topic_onboarding)) / 3
    for i in range(4)
]

query_about_security = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

print(round(cosine(query_about_security, whole_doc_vector), 4))  # 0.5955
print(round(cosine(query_about_security, topic_security), 4))    # 0.9939
```

A query about security scores much lower (0.5955) against the blurred whole-document vector than against a vector for only the security section (0.9939), even though the document contains excellent security content. The document didn't get worse; the single vector just lost its ability to point at any one of its three topics, because it has to represent all three in one fixed-size slot. Chunking each topic into its own piece and embedding each separately lets the security text get its own sharp vector instead of one smeared across the rest of the document.

sections.heading: Truncation Fails Silently and Completely
sections.body:
Truncation is worse than 'a slightly less complete vector'. It doesn't produce a fuzzier representation of the *whole* document; it produces a normal-looking vector for a *different, shorter* document: whatever fit within the token limit. Everything past the cutoff isn't represented poorly, it isn't represented at all. If the answer to a future query lives in paragraph 40 of a 60-paragraph document that got truncated at paragraph 12, no amount of clever querying or reranking downstream will surface it, because that content was never encoded into anything a similarity search could find.

This failure is dangerous because it's invisible during development. A team ingests a knowledge base, checks that search returns plausible-looking results for their test queries (which probably hit content near the start of documents, since that's what a quick smoke test probes), ships it, and months later, usually via a confused support ticket, discovers that questions about later sections of longer documents have never worked for any document. The fix isn't a smarter model. During ingestion, compare real document lengths against the embedding model's token limit and chunk anything that would otherwise be cut. A cheap guard is to count tokens with the embedding model's own tokenizer and fail loudly (or log a warning) whenever a piece exceeds the limit, so the failure becomes visible at ingestion instead of in production.

sections.heading: Chunking as a Deliberate, Offline Decision
sections.body:
Given both problems, the hard length limit and the granularity problem that exists independently of it, chunking is a first-class step in any embedding pipeline, not a workaround for unusually long documents. It happens **offline**, as part of building the index, before any embedding call: split each source document into chunks according to some strategy (the subject of the next concept), *then* embed each chunk independently and store it as its own row in the vector database, typically with metadata pointing back to the parent document (title, source path, permissions, timestamp), the same metadata filtering fields from the previous module.

One consequence to absorb early: once chunking has happened, a 'document' is no longer a retrievable unit in your index, only its chunks are. Retrieval, ranking, and filtering all operate at the chunk level. A common and easily fixed design mistake is application code that still assumes 'one document equals one search result,' when what's retrieved and ranked is one chunk out of potentially dozens from the same source document. In practice that means carrying a stable document ID on every chunk, so results can be grouped back to their source, or deduplicated when several chunks of one document land in the top k.

examples.title: Silent Truncation Loses Everything Past the Cutoff
examples.code:
def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def truncate(tokens, max_tokens):
    return tokens[:max_tokens]

def toy_embed(text, max_tokens=8):
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    truncated = truncate(tokens, max_tokens)
    seed = sum(len(t) for t in truncated)
    return [(seed % 5) / 5, (seed % 7) / 7]

document = (
    "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent driven "
    "primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March "
    "which exceeded internal projections"
)

print(len(tokenize(document)))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100))
examples.explanation: tokenize(document) shows the document is 23 tokens long, but toy_embed is called with max_tokens=8, so truncate keeps only the first 8 tokens ("The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent") and the returned vector, [0.8, 0.0], is computed from those 8 words alone. Nothing about "driven primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March which exceeded internal projections", the news in this document, reaches the seed calculation. Calling toy_embed with max_tokens=100 (enough to cover all 23 tokens) produces a different vector, [0.0, 0.0], computed from the full content. Both calls run without error and both look like ordinary embedding vectors; nothing in the output distinguishes 'a faithful representation of the document' from 'a faithful representation of the first 8 words and nothing else.'

examples.title: One Blurred Vector vs. a Sharp, Topic-Specific One
examples.code:
def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sum(x * x for x in a) ** 0.5
    nb = sum(y * y for y in b) ** 0.5
    return dot / (na * nb)

topic_billing = [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0]
topic_security = [0.0, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]
topic_onboarding = [0.0, 0.0, 0.9, 0.1]

whole_doc_vector = [
    sum(v[i] for v in (topic_billing, topic_security, topic_onboarding)) / 3
    for i in range(4)
]

query_about_security = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

print(round(cosine(query_about_security, whole_doc_vector), 4))
print(round(cosine(query_about_security, topic_security), 4))
examples.explanation: whole_doc_vector averages the three illustrative topic vectors coordinate by coordinate, standing in for what an encoder's pooling step does to a document that covers billing, security, and onboarding together. Against a query about security, that blurred vector scores only 0.5955, well below the 0.9939 the security content would score if embedded as its own chunk. The security content didn't change between the two comparisons; the only difference is whether it shared a vector with two unrelated topics or had one to itself. This is the granularity problem in miniature, and it has nothing to do with token limits: it would happen even for a model with no length restriction.

misconceptions.description: As long as the generation LLM has a huge context window (128k tokens or more), you don't need to chunk documents for RAG at all -- just embed and retrieve whole documents.
misconceptions.clarification: The generation model's context window and the embedding model's context window are two independent limits enforced by two different models. A generation model accepting 128k tokens says nothing about how many tokens the separate embedding model, which has to turn each document into a searchable vector, can accept before it truncates. And even with an embedding model that had no length limit, the retrieval-granularity problem still applies: one vector representing an entire multi-topic document is a blurrier, less discriminating representation of any single one of its topics than a vector built from that topic alone would be. Chunking addresses both problems; solving the generation model's context window addresses neither.
misconceptions.fact: The generation model's context window and the embedding model's context window are two independent limits enforced by two different models.

misconceptions.description: If a document is too long for the embedding model, truncating it just gives you a slightly less complete, slightly lower-quality vector -- still roughly representative of the whole document.
misconceptions.clarification: Truncation doesn't degrade the vector's fidelity to the whole document; it produces a vector for a different, shorter document: whatever text happened to fall before the cutoff. Content past that point isn't represented approximately; it isn't represented at all, and no later step (reranking, filtering, or anything else) can recover information that was never encoded into a vector to begin with. That is why the failure is dangerous: the vector looks ordinary, and nothing about it signals that a large fraction of the source document was discarded before the embedding call ran.
misconceptions.fact: Truncation doesn't degrade the vector's fidelity to the whole document; it produces a vector for a different, shorter document: whatever text happened to fall before the cutoff.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what does the difference between the two toy_embed calls demonstrate about truncation?
exercises.code:
def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def truncate(tokens, max_tokens):
    return tokens[:max_tokens]

def toy_embed(text, max_tokens=8):
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    truncated = truncate(tokens, max_tokens)
    seed = sum(len(t) for t in truncated)
    return [(seed % 5) / 5, (seed % 7) / 7]

document = (
    "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent driven "
    "primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March "
    "which exceeded internal projections"
)

print(len(tokenize(document)))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100))
hints: tokenize just splits on whitespace, so count the words in the document string to get the first printed number.
toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8) only ever looks at the first 8 words. Compute seed as the sum of the lengths of those 8 words: 'The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent'.
The document only has 23 words total, so max_tokens=100 doesn't change which words get used: truncate(tokens, 100) just returns the full 23-word list unchanged.
exercises.solutionExplanation: tokenize(document) splits on whitespace into 23 words, so the first print is 23. For toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8), truncate keeps only the first 8 words -- 'The', 'quarterly', 'report', 'shows', 'revenue', 'grew', 'fourteen', 'percent' -- whose lengths sum to 49; 49 % 5 = 4 so the first coordinate is 4/5 = 0.8, and 49 % 7 = 0 so the second coordinate is 0/7 = 0.0, giving [0.8, 0.0]. For toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100), truncate(tokens, 100) returns all 23 words unchanged since the document is shorter than the limit; summing the lengths of all 23 words happens to produce a seed that is an exact multiple of both 5 and 7, giving [0.0, 0.0]. The takeaway is not the numbers but that the two calls, one truncated and one not, produce two different vectors from the same input string, with nothing in either result indicating which one saw the whole document.

exercises.prompt: A knowledge-base search feature embeds each document directly with this ingestion function. After launch, users report that questions about anything mentioned after the first sentence or two of a longer document never return that document, no matter how they phrase the question. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: toy_embed has a default max_tokens=8, and ingest_document never passes anything else -- how many words of `document` actually reach the seed calculation?
Count how many words in `document` come before and after that 8-word cutoff. Is the sentence about director sign-off anywhere within the first 8 words?

The fix isn't a bigger max_tokens (that only pushes the same problem out to even longer documents). Split `document` into pieces that each fit within the limit, then embed and store every piece, not just the first one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: ingest_document calls toy_embed(text) with no max_tokens argument, so it falls back to the default of 8, and toy_embed only looks at tokens[:max_tokens], discarding everything else with no warning. The director sign-off sentence, which is what users are asking about, sits well past word 8, so it never entered the seed calculation for the single vector stored under "policy-1". That vector represents only 'Vacation requests are reviewed by the team lead.' The fix adds chunk_by_tokens, which splits the full token list into consecutive groups of at most max_tokens words, and has ingest_document embed and store every group under its own key. Now the sign-off sentence lives inside a chunk with its own vector, so a query about director sign-off has something to match. Printing the index shows the difference: the original stores one key for the document, the fixed version stores one key per chunk, and every word of the document falls inside some chunk. Increasing max_tokens would only delay the same bug until the next, slightly longer document.

assessments.prompt: A team switches their RAG pipeline's generation model to one with a 200,000-token context window and concludes they no longer need to chunk documents before indexing them. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Chunking is only relevant for documents in PDF format, not plain text.

The generation model's context window has no bearing on the embedding model's own, typically much smaller, input limit, and even without any length limit at all, embedding an entire multi-topic document into one vector still dilutes that vector's ability to represent any single topic well.
Larger context windows make embedding models slower, so chunking is still needed purely for latency reasons.
Nothing is wrong: with that much context window, whole documents can be embedded and retrieved directly.
assessments.explanation: The generation model and the embedding model are separate components with separate, independently enforced limits: upgrading the model that reads retrieved text at the end of the pipeline says nothing about the model that turns documents into searchable vectors at the beginning. Beyond that hard limit there is a second, independent reason chunking matters: even an embedding model with no length limit would produce a single vector that has to represent every topic in a long document at once, diluting its similarity to a query about any one topic. The “Nothing is wrong: with that much…” option is the flawed conclusion the question is testing for. The “Larger context windows make embedding models slower…” option invents a latency mechanism, and the generation model's window has no effect on how fast the embedding model runs. The “Chunking is only relevant for documents…” option is a fabricated, format-based distinction: chunking is about token length and topical breadth, not file type.

assessments.prompt: A document gets silently truncated by an embedding model's token limit before being embedded. Which statement best describes what happened to the resulting vector?
options: The vector represents an entirely different, shorter document -- whatever text happened to fall before the cutoff.
The vector still represents the whole document, just with slightly reduced fidelity for content near the end.
The vector's dimensionality is automatically reduced to reflect the shorter effective input, making it incompatible with un-truncated vectors stored in the same index.
The vector will contain a special marker value flagging that truncation occurred, which downstream code can check for and handle.
assessments.explanation: Truncation is a silent failure, not a degraded one: it doesn't produce a fuzzier representation of the whole document, it produces an ordinary-looking vector for a different, shorter document, whatever text fit within the limit. The “The vector still represents the whole document…” option understates the failure as reduced fidelity, when content past the cutoff is never seen by the model. The “The vector will contain a special marker…” option is fabricated: nothing in a standard embedding call flags truncation, which is why the failure is dangerous: downstream code has nothing to check. The “The vector's dimensionality is automatically reduced…” option is also fabricated: a model's output dimensionality is fixed, so truncated and untruncated calls return vectors of the same length, computed from different text.

assessments.prompt: After a team introduces chunking into their pipeline, their application code still displays results as if each one corresponds to exactly one whole source document. What design mistake does this reflect?
options: There is no mistake: chunking has no effect on what a single search result actually represents.
The mistake is purely cosmetic and has no bearing on which content actually gets embedded, searched, or ranked.
Once chunking happens, retrieval, ranking, and filtering all operate at the chunk level.
This pattern indicates the embedding model was never actually given any chunked text, and is still embedding whole documents.
assessments.explanation: Once chunking happens, a 'document' is no longer a retrievable unit in the index: only its chunks are, each stored and ranked independently, typically with metadata pointing back to the parent document. The “There is no mistake: chunking has…” option denies a consequence the lesson states outright. The “The mistake is purely cosmetic and has…” option treats a mismatch between what's retrieved (chunks) and what the UI assumes (whole documents) as harmless, when it affects how results are grouped, deduplicated, and displayed. The “This pattern indicates the embedding model…” option draws an unsupported inference: the mistake is in the application code's assumptions, not in whether ingestion chunked the text.

assessments.prompt: In the worked example, a document discussing billing, security, and onboarding roughly equally produces one pooled vector. A query about security scores only 0.5955 against that whole-document vector, but 0.9939 against a vector built from the security content alone. What causes this gap?
options: The security-related content in the document must be lower quality or less detailed than the billing and onboarding content.
The gap only appears because cosine similarity happens to be the metric used here; a different distance metric would show no meaningful difference between the two comparisons.
The whole-document vector is mathematically incorrect, reflecting a bug in how the pooling step was implemented.
Averaging together vectors representing three different topics pulls the resulting vector toward the geometric middle of all three.
assessments.explanation: The whole-document vector is the coordinate-wise average of the three topic vectors, so it sits roughly in the middle of all three: closer to each than an unrelated vector would be, but less aligned with any one than a vector built from that topic alone. That dilution, not a bug, is the mechanism the example demonstrates, which rules out the “The whole-document vector is mathematically incorrect, reflecting…” option. The “The gap only appears because cosine similarity…” option is wrong: the dilution comes from how the vector was constructed (averaging), not from the formula used to compare it afterward, so a different metric would still show a gap, though with different numbers. The “The security-related content in the document must…” option assumes a content-quality difference that has nothing to do with the mechanism, which is purely geometric: the same averaging would blur any three topics, however good the security content is.

assessments.prompt: A colleague setting up their first RAG pipeline says: 'Our generation model supports a 128k-token context window, so I'm just going to embed and retrieve whole documents instead of dealing with chunking.' Explain what you'd tell them.
assessments.modelAnswer: This plan runs into two separate problems, and the 128k generation window touches neither. First, the embedding model that builds the searchable index is a different component from the generation model, with its own input limit, commonly a few hundred to a few thousand tokens and nowhere near 128k. Many embedding libraries handle over-length input by truncating: they keep the first N tokens and drop the rest with no error or warning. Anything past the cutoff is not embedded, so a question about content late in a long document would never find that document, however large the generation window is. A question about a section on page 30 of a 50-page file is the typical casualty, and nothing in the logs would show why. Second, and this would matter even for an embedding model with unlimited input: a single vector has to represent everything a document discusses, so a document covering several subtopics ends up as a blurred average, closer to each topic than an unrelated vector would be but noticeably less close than a vector built from that topic alone. A query about one subtopic would score mediocre similarity against the blurred vector even though the document contains a great answer. Chunking solves both: splitting the document before embedding keeps each piece under the embedding model's limit and gives each subtopic its own sharp vector instead of one shared, blurred one. That also changes what the index returns: a result is now a chunk of the document, with a pointer back to its source, rather than the document itself. The generation model's large window still helps, because it lets you hand over several retrieved chunks at once, but it solves a different problem.

concepts.title: Fixed-Size, Recursive, and Semantic Chunking
concepts.description: Once documents must be split, the design question is how: fixed-size splitting is fast but blind to sentence and paragraph structure, recursive splitting respects that structure while enforcing a hard size ceiling, and semantic chunking uses the embeddings themselves to find where a topic shifts.
learningObjectives: Implement fixed-size chunking and identify its defining weakness: it cuts wherever the character or token count lands, with no regard for sentence or word boundaries.

Explain recursive chunking: splitting hierarchically along a prioritized list of separators so natural boundaries (paragraphs, then sentences, then words) are preferred whenever they fit the size budget.
Explain semantic chunking conceptually: detecting a chunk boundary from a drop in embedding similarity between adjacent sentences, rather than from any fixed character or token count.
Compare the computational cost, implementation complexity, and structure-awareness of all three strategies, and identify a document type suited to each.
Predict, given a piece of text and a chunk size, exactly where fixed-size chunking will cut, including mid-word and mid-fact splits.

sections.heading: Fixed-Size Chunking: Fast, Deterministic, and Blind
sections.body:
The simplest chunking strategy is to cut the text every N characters (or N tokens):

```python
def fixed_size_chunk(text, size):
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), size)]
```

It has real advantages: a few lines of code, no dependencies, fast enough to run over an enormous corpus without a second thought, and fully deterministic (the same text and size always produce the same chunks), which makes the resulting index easy to debug and reason about. But it has no concept of a sentence, a word, or a complete thought. It cuts wherever the count lands, whatever it's in the middle of.

```python
text = (
    "The vendor invoice was flagged for review because "
    "the tax identification number on file did not match "
    "government records."
)
for chunk in fixed_size_chunk(text, 50):
    print(repr(chunk))
```

Running this splits the passage into 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ', 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', and 'h government records.' The *reason* the invoice was flagged (the tax ID mismatch) is separated from the fact that it *was* flagged, and the word 'match' is cut in half between the second and third chunks. Neither chunk, embedded and stored on its own, answers 'why was this invoice flagged?': the first says something was flagged but not why, and the second gives a reason without saying what it applies to. This isn't a contrived edge case; it's the default behavior of cutting on a raw count, applied to ordinary prose.

sections.heading: Recursive Chunking: A Prioritized List of Separators
Semantic Chunking: Boundaries Discovered From Meaning, Not Position
sections.body:
Recursive chunking's separators (blank lines, sentence punctuation, whitespace) are syntactic guesses about where a topic probably changes. For content where topic shifts don't line up with those markers, such as meeting transcripts, chat logs, and rambling notes, even a well-implemented recursive splitter is following formatting conventions that may have nothing to do with where the subject changes.

**Semantic chunking** works differently: embed each sentence, compute the similarity between every pair of *adjacent* sentence embeddings, and treat a sharp drop as evidence that the topic shifted. Cut a boundary there, whether or not it falls near a paragraph break.

```python
sentence_similarities = [0.95, 0.92, 0.40, 0.90, 0.93, 0.35, 0.88]
# similarity between sentence i and sentence i+1, for 8 sentences

def find_boundaries(sims, threshold):
    return [i + 1 for i, s in enumerate(sims) if s < threshold]

print(find_boundaries(sentence_similarities, threshold=0.6))  # [3, 6]
```

Two sharp drops, between sentences 3 and 4 and between sentences 6 and 7, mark two topic shifts and split the 8 sentences into three coherent groups: sentences 1-3, 4-6, and 7-8. The price is extra compute: every sentence must be embedded in a preprocessing pass before the chunk-level embeddings are computed, on top of what those cost. That makes the pipeline materially more expensive than fixed-size or recursive chunking, which need no model calls to decide where to cut. The threshold also needs tuning per embedding model; 0.6 only suits these toy numbers.

sections.heading: Choosing Among the Three
sections.body:
None of the three is universally best: they trade cost against structure-awareness, and the right default depends on the content. Fixed-size chunking is reasonable for short, homogeneous text where an occasional bad cut is low-stakes, or as a quick prototype. Recursive chunking is the sensible default for most production pipelines: it costs nothing beyond string operations, and for well-formatted documents (Markdown, docs with clear headings, prose with paragraph breaks) respecting the existing structure captures most of the benefit semantic chunking would provide, at a fraction of the cost. Semantic chunking earns its extra expense when topic shifts are frequent and don't align with any syntactic marker in the source. Whichever you pick, the quickest sanity check is to print a sample of chunks and read them: broken sentences and orphaned fragments are obvious by eye.

A common and costly mistake is running fixed-size or naive recursive chunking over structured technical content, such as Markdown with code fences or source code, without a structure-specific separator (a code-fence delimiter, or a function or class boundary) high in the separator list. Splitting on paragraph breaks or raw character counts can cut a code block in half and embed a fragment that isn't valid code and means nothing out of context. It's much easier to prevent up front than to notice later, because the chunk still embeds and stores without any error. Text-splitter libraries such as LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter ship language-aware separator presets for this reason, so check what your splitter offers before writing separators by hand.

examples.title: Fixed-Size Chunking Cuts the Reason Away From the Fact
examples.explanation: The three resulting chunks are 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ', 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', and 'h government records.'. The word 'match' is split into 'matc' and 'h', but the more damaging split is semantic: the first chunk says an invoice was flagged, the second gives a reason (a tax ID mismatch), and neither connects the two. A query like 'why was the invoice flagged?' needs both chunks, and a system that retrieves only the single best-matching chunk would plausibly surface only half the story.

examples.title: Recursive Chunking Falls Back to Whole-Word Boundaries
examples.explanation: The first two paragraphs (23 and 46 characters) are under the 60-character budget, so each survives as one untouched chunk. The third paragraph is far too long, so recursive_chunk recurses into it: there's no '. ' inside it (it's one long sentence), so it falls through to splitting on spaces, producing three word-boundary-respecting pieces of length 60, 58, and 24. Every cut lands between two whole words, a guarantee fixed-size chunking cannot offer. The last chunk is short (24) because the greedy loop flushes as soon as the next word would overflow the budget, so chunk sizes vary, which is normal for structure-aware splitting.

examples.title: Finding Topic Boundaries From a Drop in Similarity
examples.code:
sentence_similarities = [0.95, 0.92, 0.40, 0.90, 0.93, 0.35, 0.88]

def find_boundaries(sims, threshold):
    return [i + 1 for i, s in enumerate(sims) if s < threshold]

print(find_boundaries(sentence_similarities, threshold=0.6))
examples.explanation: sentence_similarities[i] is the similarity between sentence i+1 and sentence i+2 in a hypothetical eight-sentence passage. Two values, 0.40 (between sentences 3 and 4) and 0.35 (between sentences 6 and 7), fall well below the 0.6 threshold, so find_boundaries reports [3, 6]: a boundary after sentence 3 and another after sentence 6. Every other adjacent pair stays at 0.88 or above, so the topic is continuing there. The three resulting chunks (sentences 1-3, 4-6, and 7-8) came from where the meaning shifted, with no paragraph break, punctuation mark, or fixed size consulted.

misconceptions.description: Recursive chunking's list of separators makes it just as 'smart' or meaning-aware as semantic chunking -- they're both sophisticated alternatives to naive fixed-size chunking.
misconceptions.clarification: Recursive chunking is structure-aware, not meaning-aware: every separator in its list (a blank line, a period and space, a plain space) is a fixed syntactic marker chosen in advance without looking at what the text means. It works because paragraphs and sentences usually correlate with meaningful structure in well-formatted writing, but that correlation is a convenience for typical prose, not something recursive chunking measures. Semantic chunking measures meaning through embedding similarity between adjacent sentences, and it's the only one of the two that would still find the topic boundary where paragraph breaks and topic shifts don't line up.

misconceptions.description: Since semantic chunking uses embeddings to decide where to cut, it always produces meaningfully better retrieval than fixed-size or recursive chunking, so it's worth using everywhere.
misconceptions.clarification: Semantic chunking's extra cost (an embedding call per sentence in a dedicated preprocessing pass, on top of the chunk-level embeddings) has to be worth it for the corpus. For well-structured documents (technical docs, articles, anything with paragraph breaks and clear headings), recursive chunking already captures most of the same benefit, because syntactic and topical boundaries mostly coincide. Semantic chunking's advantage is sharpest where that coincidence breaks down, as in unstructured transcripts, chat logs, and rambling notes, where a speaker can change subject mid-paragraph. Paying its cost on content without that problem buys very little over the cheaper recursive approach.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and which specific word ends up split across a chunk boundary?
hints: fixed_size_chunk just slices the string every 50 characters, with no awareness of where words begin or end, so count characters, not words, to find each cut point.
The first chunk is text[0:50], the second is text[50:100], and so on -- write out the string and mark the 50th and 100th character positions.
Once you have the three chunk strings, look at where the second one ends and the third one begins -- is there a complete word straddling that boundary?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ', then 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', then 'h government records.'; the word 'match' is split into 'matc' and 'h'.
exercises.solutionExplanation: text[0:50] is 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ' (including the trailing space, since the cut is purely by character count). text[50:100] continues with 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', stopping one character short of finishing 'match'. text[100:150] (shorter than 50 characters, since the string ends there) picks up the leftover 'h' followed by ' government records.'. fixed_size_chunk never looks at word boundaries: it was luck that the first cut landed on a space. The second cut landing mid-word is the more typical outcome of counting characters with no regard for what they spell. (The first cut is the lucky one: character 50 happens to be the space after 'because'.)

exercises.prompt: Implement `recursive_chunk(text, max_size, separators)`: try splitting `text` on `separators[0]` first; if that produces only one piece (the separator never appears), recurse with `separators[1:]` on the whole text. Otherwise, greedily reassemble the pieces into chunks that each stay within `max_size`, recursing into any single piece that is itself still too long. Then chunk the sample document with separators ["\n\n", ". ", " "] and max_size=60.
exercises.code:
def split_on(text, sep):
    return [p for p in text.split(sep) if p]

def recursive_chunk(text, max_size, separators):
    # TODO: implement as described in the prompt.
    pass

doc = (
    "Paragraph one is short.\n\n"
    "Paragraph two is also fairly short and simple.\n\n"
    "Paragraph three is much longer and goes on for quite a while "
    "describing many details that would not normally fit into a "
    "small chunk size at all."
)
for chunk in recursive_chunk(doc, 60, ["\n\n", ". ", " "]):
    print(len(chunk), repr(chunk))
hints: Base case: if len(text) <= max_size, or there are no separators left to try, just return [text]; there's nothing left to split.
Split on separators[0]. If that gives back only one piece, the separator didn't appear anywhere in this text, so recurse immediately with separators[1:] instead.

Otherwise, walk the pieces and greedily glue them back together (re-inserting the separator between them) into a running `current` chunk, flushing `current` into the results list whenever adding the next piece would exceed max_size, and recursing into any individual piece that's still too long on its own, using the remaining separators.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Splitting doc on "\n\n" produces three pieces, the three paragraphs, so the function goes to the greedy reassembly loop rather than recursing immediately. The first two paragraphs (23 and 46 characters) each fit under 60 on their own and are flushed as chunks. The third paragraph is about 144 characters, so instead of being force-cut at 60 it goes back through recursive_chunk with the remaining separators [". ", " "]. There's no ". " inside it, so the recursion falls through to splitting on " " and reassembles words into three chunks of length 60, 58, and 24, none cutting through a word. The result is five chunks: two whole paragraphs plus three word-respecting pieces of the oversized third.

exercises.prompt: A fixed-size chunker should split text into chunks of `size` characters where each chunk overlaps the previous one by `overlap` characters. For a 10-character text with size 4 and overlap 2 it should produce 4 chunks ending with 'ghij', but the last characters are missing. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
def chunk(text, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap
    chunks = []
    for start in range(0, len(text) - size, step):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + size])
    return chunks

print(chunk("abcdefghij", 4, 2))   # expected: ['abcd', 'cdef', 'efgh', 'ghij']
hints: Which start positions does range produce for this input?
The last full chunk starts at len(text) - size; is that value included by range?
range stops before its end value, so the end needs to be one larger.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `range(0, len(text) - size, step)` excludes its end value, so the start position 6 (the last full chunk 'ghij') was never generated and the end of every document was dropped from the index. Adding 1 to the end includes the final start. The extra check also appends a tail chunk when the step does not land exactly on the end, so no characters are lost for other lengths. Off-by-one errors in chunkers are dangerous because nothing crashes: the missing text just never shows up in search results.

assessments.prompt: What is the key difference between recursive chunking and semantic chunking?
options: Recursive chunking requires a trained embedding model; semantic chunking does not.
They are two names for the same algorithm, differing only in implementation language.
Recursive chunking is only for code, and semantic chunking is only for prose.

Recursive chunking splits on a prioritized list of fixed, syntactic separators (paragraph breaks, then sentences, then words); semantic chunking measures embedding similarity between adjacent sentences and cuts wherever that similarity drops, regardless of syntax.
assessments.explanation: Recursive chunking never looks at meaning: it works from fixed, predetermined syntactic markers, falling back down its separator list only when a higher-priority one doesn't produce small enough pieces. Semantic chunking embeds individual sentences and cuts where the *meaning* shifts, which can happen anywhere, independent of paragraph or sentence boundaries. The “Recursive chunking is only for code…” option invents a content-type restriction that doesn't exist for either strategy. The “They are two names for the same…” option is wrong because they produce different boundaries on the same input whenever syntactic and semantic structure diverge. The “Recursive chunking requires a trained embedding model…” option has the dependency backwards: semantic chunking is the one that needs an embedding model, to measure sentence-to-sentence similarity, while recursive chunking needs only string splitting.

assessments.prompt: Despite being blind to sentence and word boundaries, fixed-size chunking has some genuine, legitimate advantages according to the explanation. Which of the following is one of them?
options: It automatically detects and avoids cutting through Markdown code blocks or other structured content.
It requires no dependencies, runs fast enough over an enormous corpus without a second thought, and is fully deterministic -- the same text and size always produce exactly the same chunks.
It improves its cut points over time by training a small classifier on which boundaries produced better retrieval results, so the chunks it produces keep getting better as more queries are answered.
It always produces chunks that are more semantically coherent than recursive chunking would produce on the same text.
assessments.explanation: Fixed-size chunking's advantages are that it's a few lines of code with no dependencies, fast enough for an enormous corpus, and fully deterministic, which keeps the resulting index easy to debug. The “It always produces chunks that are more…” option is false: fixed-size chunking is the least structure-aware of the three strategies. The “It automatically detects and avoids cutting through…” option describes the failure fixed-size (and naive recursive) chunking is prone to on technical content, not something it avoids. The “It improves its cut points over time…” option describes a learning mechanism fixed-size chunking doesn't have: it applies the same rule (cut every N characters) regardless of feedback.

assessments.prompt: In recursive chunking, suppose splitting a document on the highest-priority separator (a blank line between paragraphs) leaves one resulting paragraph still too large for the size budget. What happens next?
options: The entire document is discarded and re-processed from scratch using only whitespace splitting.
That oversized paragraph is force-cut at the exact character limit, regardless of word boundaries -- the same behavior fixed-size chunking would produce.

That specific oversized paragraph is recursively split again using the next separator down the prioritized list (such as sentence-ending punctuation, then plain whitespace), continuing to respect structure rather than falling back to an arbitrary character cut.
The oversized paragraph is embedded exactly as-is, exceeding the size budget, since recursive chunking has no hard ceiling on chunk size.
assessments.explanation: This is the core of recursive chunking: only the piece that's still too large is recursed into, using the remaining lower-priority separators in order (sentence punctuation, then whitespace as a last resort), so structure is respected as long as possible before falling back to a less natural boundary. The “That oversized paragraph is force-cut…” option describes fixed-size chunking, which recursive chunking avoids until every other separator is exhausted. The “The entire document is discarded and re-processed…” option invents a wasteful restart: only the oversized piece recurses. The “The oversized paragraph is embedded exactly as-is…” option is wrong because the recursion exists to keep chunks within the size budget; recursive chunking enforces a hard ceiling, and it just tries harder than fixed-size chunking to respect structure while doing so.

assessments.prompt: Why does semantic chunking require materially more compute than either fixed-size or recursive chunking?
options: It requires embedding every individual sentence as a dedicated preprocessing pass, on top of whatever chunk-level embeddings eventually get computed -- whereas neither fixed-size nor recursive chunking requires any model calls at all to decide where to cut.
It requires running the generation LLM once for every candidate boundary to judge whether a topic shift actually occurred there.
It only works with the largest and most expensive embedding models available, unlike fixed-size or recursive chunking, which can use any model.
It requires re-embedding the entire corpus multiple times in a loop until the detected boundaries stop changing.
assessments.explanation: Semantic chunking's extra cost is that it embeds every sentence individually to compute adjacent-sentence similarity, in a separate pass before the chunk-level embeddings are computed. Fixed-size and recursive chunking decide where to cut with zero model calls, which is why they're so much cheaper. The “It requires re-embedding the entire corpus multiple…” option invents an iterative loop that isn't part of the mechanism: boundaries come from one pass of adjacent-sentence similarities. The “It only works with the largest…” option is a fabricated constraint, since the sentence-level embeddings could use any embedding model. The “It requires running the generation LLM once…” option confuses semantic chunking with the generation LLM, which plays no role in choosing chunk boundaries.

assessments.prompt: A teammate is about to run naive fixed-size chunking over a corpus of technical documentation that includes Markdown code blocks. Explain what could go wrong, and what you'd recommend instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fixed-size chunking cuts on a raw character or token count with no awareness of what it's cutting through, and a Markdown code block is where that does the most damage. A cut can land in the middle of a function, splitting it across two chunks that are each a broken code fragment, and each would embed into a vector for a confusing partial snippet rather than the function it came from. Worse, nothing signals the problem: the chunker runs without error, the fragment is embedded and stored like any other chunk, and nobody notices until retrieval is oddly poor for code-related queries. I'd switch to recursive chunking with a separator list that puts code-fence boundaries (triple backticks) ahead of generic paragraph and sentence splitting, so that wherever possible a whole code block stays intact as its own chunk (or grouped with the prose around it). If individual functions or blocks are still too large, a further split on function or class boundaries, rather than raw line count, keeps each piece syntactically meaningful, which matters for how well it embeds and matches a query.

concepts.title: Chunk Size, Overlap, and the Precision/Context Tradeoff
concepts.description: Chunk size and overlap are the two knobs that control how well retrieval works in practice. A chunk too small severs a fact from the context it needs, a chunk too large dilutes relevance the way an undivided document does, and overlap mitigates boundary damage without eliminating it, at a measurable storage and latency cost.
learningObjectives: Explain the two-sided failure mode of chunk size: chunks too small losing necessary surrounding context, versus chunks too large diluting relevance, and connect the 'too large' case back to the granularity problem.
Explain what overlap is mechanically, and how it increases the chance that a fact sitting near a chunk boundary ends up whole in at least one stored chunk.
Compute how the number of chunks -- and therefore embedding and storage cost -- produced from a fixed-length document changes as overlap increases, for a fixed chunk size.
Describe an evidence-based process for choosing chunk size and overlap for a real corpus, rather than adopting a library's default values unexamined.
Diagnose, given a specific retrieval failure, whether it is better explained by chunk size being too large, too small, or by insufficient overlap.

sections.heading: Two Failure Modes on the Same Knob
sections.body:
Chunk size sits on a single numeric axis but fails in two different directions, so 'smaller is safer' isn't a rule you can lean on. A chunk that's **too small** can sever a fact from the context that gives it meaning: a table row without its header row, a sentence like 'the request was ultimately denied' without whatever preceded it that says which request, or a single clause of a larger conditional statement with the condition itself sitting in the previous, unretrieved chunk. A chunk that's small enough to be sharply on-topic can still be useless if it's too small to be *self-contained*.

A chunk that's **too large** runs into the granularity problem from the first concept, at a smaller scale than a whole document: the more distinct ideas a chunk covers, the more its one pooled vector has to represent at once, and the less sharply it represents any one. A chunk covering five loosely related paragraphs is the same problem as embedding a 50-page document as one vector, with slightly fewer topics doing the diluting. Neither failure mode raises an error; both just produce worse retrieval, and the cause only becomes clear when you look at what was retrieved and what it was missing. That is the habit to build: when an answer is wrong, read the retrieved chunks before touching the model or the prompt.

sections.heading: What Overlap Buys You
sections.body:
**Overlap** means each chunk after the first repeats the tail end of the chunk before it, rather than starting exactly where the previous one left off:

```python
def chunk_with_overlap(text, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]
```

The window advances by `size - overlap` instead of the full `size`, so the last `overlap` characters of one chunk reappear as the first `overlap` characters of the next. This rescues facts that would otherwise land on a chunk boundary and get cut in half:

```python
text = (
    "Refunds are approved only when the return request is "
    "submitted within 30 days of the delivery date, no exceptions."
)

no_overlap = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=75, overlap=0)
with_overlap = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=75, overlap=20)

print(any("30 days" in c for c in no_overlap))    # False
print(any("30 days" in c for c in with_overlap))  # True
```

With no overlap, a 75-character chunk size happens to cut through the middle of '30 days': 'within 30 da' ends one chunk, 'ys of the delivery date...' begins the next, and the number-plus-unit never appears whole in either. With a 20-character overlap, the second chunk starts 20 characters earlier, early enough to include '30 days' whole with context on both sides, even though the *first* chunk still ends at the same awkward spot. Overlap doesn't fix every boundary; it adds a shifted chunk that has a good chance of containing whole whatever the unshifted boundary cut through.

sections.heading: Overlap's Cost: More Chunks, More Storage, More Redundant Retrieval
sections.body:
Overlap isn't free, and the cost is easy to compute ahead of time. For a document of length `L`, chunk size `S`, and overlap `O`, the window advances `S - O` characters per step, so the number of chunks is roughly `L / (S - O)`:

```python
import math

def chunk_count(length, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap
    return math.ceil(max(length - overlap, 0) / step) if length > 0 else 0

for overlap in (0, 50, 100):
    print(overlap, chunk_count(1000, 200, overlap))

# 0   5
# 50  7
# 100 9
```

For a 1,000-character document and 200-character chunks, going from no overlap to a 100-character overlap (half the chunk size) nearly doubles the chunk count, from 5 to 9. Each extra chunk is another embedding to compute at ingestion, another row to store, and another candidate for future top-k results, so a query is more likely to retrieve two or three heavily overlapping chunks that repeat the same text instead of three or four distinct pieces of information. Retrieval can merge or deduplicate such neighbors before building the prompt, but that adds another step to maintain. That cost lands on the generation LLM's limited context budget: tokens spent on near-duplicate text aren't spent on useful new content.

sections.heading: Choosing Values by Measurement, Not by Habit
sections.body:
There's no universal chunk size or overlap, for the same reason there's no universal `nprobe` or `ef_search` from the ANN indexing module: the right value depends on your documents and your queries, not on a number that worked for someone else's corpus. The process mirrors recall tuning: assemble a set of real (or realistically representative) questions, each paired with the source text that should answer it. Then for several candidate chunk_size/overlap settings, check whether that source span ends up fully inside a single retrieved chunk, and ultimately check end-task answer accuracy in the full RAG pipeline, not whether a human skimming the chunks thinks they 'look reasonable.'

A chunk size in the low hundreds of tokens with an overlap around 10-20% of that size is a common place to *start* for general prose, not a value to adopt without checking it against your own data. Measure sizes in the units the embedding model uses (tokens, not characters), since its limit is in tokens, and a 500-character chunk can be well under or over that depending on the language and the text. Dense legal contracts, short chat messages, and long-form articles differ enough in structure that a setting tuned for one shouldn't be assumed to carry over to another, even within the same product.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.body: Three mistakes show up often. The first is treating 'bigger chunks' as strictly safer on the theory that more context can only help: past a certain size, a bigger chunk hurts retrieval precision, not just cost. The second is using zero overlap by default because it's the parameter's most obvious value, then being surprised when an important fact is split across the wrong boundary; overlap is a worthwhile mitigation, not an optional nicety. The third is assuming one chunk_size/overlap setting applies uniformly to a corpus that contains structurally different document types, when a setting suited to long dense prose may be badly mismatched to short choppy content in the same index.

examples.title: Overlap Rescues a Fact That a Bare Boundary Would Have Split
examples.explanation: With overlap=0, the two chunks are 'Refunds are approved only when the return request is submitted within 30 da' and 'ys of the delivery date, no exceptions.' The number-plus-unit '30 days' is split into 'da' and 'ys' across the boundary, so neither chunk contains it whole, and a query about the return window would find no chunk with the complete phrase. With overlap=20, the first chunk is identical (it still ends where it did before), but the second chunk starts 20 characters earlier, at 'bmitted within 30 days of the delivery date, no exceptions.', which contains '30 days' whole with context on both sides. (A tiny third chunk, 'ons.', also appears, a side effect of this simple loop.) The fact was rescued not by fixing the original boundary but by adding a shifted chunk that never hit it.

examples.title: Overlap's Cost: Chunk Count Grows as Overlap Grows
examples.explanation: For a 1,000-character document and 200-character chunks, chunk_count climbs from 5 with no overlap to 7 with a 50-character overlap to 9 with a 100-character overlap (half the chunk size), nearly double the original. Each of the 4 extra chunks needs its own embedding, and several substantially repeat text a neighbor also contains, so a top-k retrieval for this document is more likely to return two or three chunks that are mostly the same text, crowding out chunks that would have added new information.

misconceptions.description: Bigger chunks are strictly safer than smaller ones, since they include more surrounding context and can only help retrieval, never hurt it.
misconceptions.clarification: Past a certain point, a bigger chunk hurts retrieval precision, for the same reason an undivided document does: the more distinct ideas packed into one chunk, the more its single pooled vector has to represent all of them at once, diluting how sharply it represents any one of them. A query about one specific idea inside an overly large chunk scores a noticeably lower similarity than it would against a smaller, more tightly-focused chunk covering just that idea -- so 'more context per chunk' trades away retrieval precision, it doesn't purely add safety margin.

misconceptions.description: Adding overlap between chunks eliminates the risk of an important fact being split across a chunk boundary.
misconceptions.clarification: Overlap reduces but does not eliminate that risk: it adds extra shifted chunks that have a good chance of missing the boundary their unshifted neighbors hit, without guaranteeing every fact stays intact. A fact longer than the overlap window, or one that happens to span more than one boundary, can still end up split even with overlap in place. Overlap is a worthwhile mitigation with a measurable storage and redundant-retrieval cost, not a way to make chunk boundaries stop mattering.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what does the trend across the three overlap values tell you about overlap's cost?
hints: step = size - overlap, so for overlap=0, step=200; for overlap=50, step=150; for overlap=100, step=100.
chunk_count computes math.ceil((length - overlap) / step) -- work out (1000 - overlap) / step for each of the three overlap values first.
Notice step shrinks as overlap grows, while the numerator (1000 - overlap) shrinks much more slowly -- so the ratio, and therefore the chunk count, has to grow.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For overlap=0: step=200, so chunk_count = ceil((1000-0)/200) = ceil(5.0) = 5. For overlap=50: step=150, chunk_count = ceil((1000-50)/150) = ceil(950/150) = ceil(6.33) = 7. For overlap=100: step=100, chunk_count = ceil((1000-100)/100) = ceil(900/100) = 9. As overlap grows from 0 to 100 (half the chunk size), the number of chunks needed to cover the same 1000-character document nearly doubles, from 5 to 9, because a bigger overlap means each chunk advances a shorter distance past the previous one, so more are needed to cover the same length. The formula is an approximation: the simple loop in chunk_with_overlap also emits a small trailing chunk that duplicates text already covered, as the 'ons.' chunk in the first example shows. Every extra chunk is an extra embedding to compute, store, and potentially retrieve alongside near-duplicate neighbors.

exercises.prompt: This chunking function is supposed to create overlapping chunks so that a fact near a boundary is likely to appear whole in at least one chunk. Instead, testing reveals it's doing the opposite -- entire stretches of the source text never appear in ANY chunk at all. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
def chunk_with_overlap(text, size, overlap):
    step = size + overlap  # advance further per chunk to "add" overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

text = "AAAAABBBBBCCCCCDDDDDEEEEEFFFFFGGGGGHHHHHIIIIIJJJJJ"
chunks = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=10, overlap=5)
for c in chunks:
    print(repr(c))
# CCCCC, FFFFF, and IIIII never appear in any chunk at all
hints: Overlap is supposed to make consecutive chunks share some trailing/leading text -- does advancing FURTHER per chunk (step = size + overlap) make chunks share more text, or less?
Work out what index each chunk starts at with step = size + overlap = 15, and compare that to where the previous chunk actually ended (start + size = start + 10). Is there a gap?
The step between chunk starts needs to be SMALLER than the chunk size for there to be any overlap at all -- that means subtracting overlap from size, not adding it.
exercises.solutionCode:
def chunk_with_overlap(text, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap  # advance LESS than a full chunk width, to overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

text = "AAAAABBBBBCCCCCDDDDDEEEEEFFFFFGGGGGHHHHHIIIIIJJJJJ"
chunks = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=10, overlap=5)
for c in chunks:
    print(repr(c))
# every 5-letter group now appears in at least one chunk, several appear in two
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is step = size + overlap, which advances each chunk's start further than the chunk's width (10 + 5 = 15, but each chunk covers only 10 characters), leaving a 5-character gap between chunks instead of a 5-character overlap. That's why 'CCCCC', 'FFFFF', and 'IIIII' vanish: they fall inside the gaps and no chunk's window captures them. This is more serious than a boundary cutting a fact in half, because the content is absent from the index. The fix, step = size - overlap = 5, starts each chunk only 5 characters after the previous one began (the chunk width is 10), so consecutive chunks share 5 characters. Every letter group is captured by at least one chunk and several by two, which is the intended overlap behavior.

assessments.prompt: A team, worried about facts getting split across chunk boundaries, sets their chunk size very large -- each chunk now covers what used to be 8-10 smaller chunks. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Nothing changes, since chunk size only affects storage cost, not retrieval quality.

Retrieval precision gets worse: each chunk's single pooled vector now has to represent many more distinct ideas at once, diluting its similarity to a query about any one specific idea -- the same granularity problem that motivated chunking whole documents in the first place, just recurring at a smaller scale.
The embedding model will reject chunks above a certain size with an explicit error, so the team will find out immediately if this is a problem.
Retrieval quality improves unconditionally, since larger chunks contain more context and are strictly safer.
assessments.explanation: Increasing chunk size doesn't just risk hitting an embedding model's token limit: well before that, a chunk covering many distinct ideas produces one vector that has to represent all of them, a smaller-scale recurrence of the whole-document granularity problem from the first concept. The “Retrieval quality improves unconditionally, since larger chunks…” option ignores that dilution. The “Nothing changes, since chunk size only affects…” option is wrong because chunk size affects both storage cost and retrieval precision. The “The embedding model will reject chunks above…” option is wrong because many embedding pipelines truncate without raising an error, which is why the failure can go unnoticed rather than being 'found out immediately.'

assessments.prompt: A retrieved chunk contains only the sentence "The request was ultimately denied." with no surrounding text -- a reader has no way to tell which request, or why. What specific failure mode does this illustrate?
options: This is evidence that the embedding model silently truncated the input before embedding it.
This indicates the overlap setting was too high, causing excessive redundant retrieval, so lowering that setting until no two chunks share any text would fix this problem.
The chunk is too large, causing its pooled vector to dilute across too many unrelated topics.
The chunk is too small to be self-contained -- it's sharply on-topic (it really is about a denial), but severed from the context that actually gives the fact its meaning.
assessments.explanation: This is the 'too small' failure mode: a chunk can be small enough to be sharply on-topic and still be useless because it isn't self-contained, missing the preceding context (which request, what grounds) needed to understand the fact. The “The chunk is too large, causing…” option describes the opposite failure, dilution from too many topics, which doesn't apply to a chunk that is too narrow. The “This indicates the overlap setting…” option misattributes the problem to overlap, which affects whether a fact is duplicated across boundaries, not whether one small chunk lacks context. The “This is evidence that the embedding model…” option describes an unrelated failure, input exceeding a hard token limit.

assessments.prompt: As overlap increases toward roughly half of the chunk size, what happens to the total number of chunks produced from a fixed-length document, and what is the direct downstream consequence?
options: The chunk count stays exactly the same regardless of overlap, since overlap changes what each chunk contains, not how many chunks there are.
The chunk count decreases, since a larger overlap means fewer distinct chunks are needed to cover the same document.
The chunk count increases substantially (potentially nearly doubling).
The chunk count increases, but only for documents that are shorter than the configured chunk size itself.
assessments.explanation: Because the step between consecutive chunk starts is size minus overlap, a bigger overlap makes each chunk advance less, so more chunks are needed to cover the same document; the worked numbers show the count nearly doubling (5 to 9) as overlap grows from 0 to half the chunk size. Each extra chunk is an embedding and storage cost (and a row to keep in sync when the source changes), and several substantially repeat text a neighbor contains, crowding out distinct information from a limited top-k. The “The chunk count decreases, since a larger…” option has the relationship backwards. The “The chunk count stays exactly the same…” option ignores that overlap changes the step size and therefore the count, not just chunk content. The “The chunk count increases, but only…” option invents a length-dependent exception that isn't part of how chunk_count behaves.

assessments.prompt: A team adds a modest overlap to their chunking pipeline and concludes that important facts near a chunk boundary can no longer end up split across two chunks. Is this conclusion correct?
options: No: overlap reduces this risk, by adding extra, shifted chunks that have a good chance of not hitting the exact same boundary as their un-shifted neighbors, but a fact longer than the overlap window, or one that spans more than one boundary, can still end up split even with overlap in place.
No: overlap has no effect whatsoever on boundary-splitting risk; it only changes storage and embedding cost.
Yes: any nonzero overlap fully guarantees that every fact stays intact within at least one chunk, no matter how long the fact is.
Yes, but only for chunks built from English-language text; other languages are unaffected by overlap.
assessments.explanation: Overlap mitigates boundary damage without eliminating it: it adds shifted chunks that often, but not always, avoid the same cut point, so a fact that's long relative to the overlap window, or that spans multiple boundaries, can still be split. The “Yes: any nonzero overlap fully guarantees…” option overclaims a guarantee the mechanism doesn't provide. The “No: overlap has no effect whatsoever…” option understates overlap's benefit (it rescued '30 days' in the worked example). The “Yes, but only for chunks built…” option introduces a language distinction with no basis in how overlap works, which is purely about character or token position.

assessments.prompt: A colleague building a new RAG pipeline asks how they should pick chunk_size and overlap for their specific document collection, since every blog post they've read recommends different numbers. Explain the process you'd recommend instead of picking a number from a blog post.
assessments.modelAnswer: There's no universally correct chunk_size or overlap, because the right values depend on the structure of your documents and the questions your users ask. The same is true of nprobe or ef_search for an ANN index, and the process is similar: measure against your own data instead of adopting someone else's tuned value. I'd start by assembling a representative set of real (or realistically written) questions, each paired with the span of source text that should answer it. Then, for a handful of candidate chunk_size and overlap settings, I'd check two things. First, whether the answer span ends up fully inside a single chunk at each setting (a chunk size too small will often sever it from the context that makes it a complete answer). Second, and more important, end-task accuracy: run the full retrieval-plus-generation pipeline and check whether the final answers are correct, since a chunk that looks fine to a human skimming it can still perform differently once it competes against other chunks in a similarity ranking. I'd start from a modest chunk size (a few hundred tokens) with overlap around 10-20% as a starting point to tune from, not as the answer, and I'd watch for documents in the collection that differ structurally (dense legal text versus short chat messages, say), since a setting tuned for one type shouldn't be assumed to fit another in the same index. I'd re-run the measurement whenever the corpus's document types shift meaningfully, for the same reason ANN recall tuning has to be re-checked after a data distribution shift.

assessments.prompt: Your RAG system answers questions about long legal contracts poorly: retrieved chunks are either fragments missing the key clause or huge passages that drown the answer. How would you choose and validate a chunking strategy?
assessments.modelAnswer: Chunk size trades precision against context. Small chunks embed a focused meaning and rank well, but can cut a clause from the definitions or conditions it depends on; huge chunks keep context but dilute the embedding so the relevant sentence ranks poorly and the prompt fills with noise. For contracts, chunk along structure (sections and clauses) rather than fixed character counts, add modest overlap, and attach metadata such as section title and contract ID to each chunk, possibly prepending the heading to the text being embedded. Consider small-to-big retrieval: embed small chunks for matching, then return the surrounding section to the model. Validate with a golden set of real questions and the clause that answers each, measuring recall at k and answer quality across a few chunk sizes, and pick the configuration with the best results rather than guessing.
